## Article

- Citation and DOI: Joel S, Teper R, MacDonald G. People overestimate their willingness to reject potential romantic partners by overlooking their concern for other people. Psychol Sci. 2014 Dec;25(12):2233-40. doi: 10.1177/0956797614552828. Epub 2014 Oct 24. PMID: 25344347.
DOI: 10.1177/0956797614552828
- Data/materials repository URL: https://github.com/B-Sevchik/ps3/tree/master/ps3/Group%20A/Choice%201/data
- Part A (known case) or Part B (a classmate's project paper): Part A

## Target outcomes

Written **before** opening the data. Quote each from the paper. In Part B, one of these must
be the project's key effect.

| # | Target outcome (quoted) | Paper value(s) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | "confirm that participants indeed viewed the potential date as unattractive"| "A paired-samples t test indicated that participants found the potential date (M = 4.48) to be significantly less attractive than themselves (M = 6.08), t(103) = 6.77, p < .001." |
| 2 | "primary hypothesis that participants would be more reluctant to reject the unattractive date when they believed the situation to be real rather than hypothetical" | "A chi-square test of independence indicated that participants were significantly less likely to reject the unattractive potential date in the real condition compared with the hypothetical condition, χ2(1, N = 132) = 6.77, p = .009"|
| 3 | "potential effects of the experimental manipulation (real condition vs. hypothetical condition) on participants’ self-reported motives regarding their decision"|"Results of a Wilks’s lambda multivariate analysis of variance (ANOVA) were significant, F(2, 129) = 4.85, p = .009, ηp2 = .07." |
| 4 |"whether participants’ willingness to reject the incompatible potential dates differed on the basis of whether they believed the situation to be real or hypothetical" |"A test of independence indicated that participants in the real condition were significantly less likely to reject the unattractive potential date than were participants in the hypothetical condition, χ2(1, N = 99) = 8.22, p = .004." |
| 5 |"whether the experimental manipulation (real condition vs. hypothetical condition) affected participants’ self-reported motives for their choices" |"Results of a Wilks’s lambda multivariate ANOVA were significant, F(2, 96) = 3.71, p = .03, ηp2 = .07." |
| 6 |"whether other-focused motives was a mediator of the effect of condition (hypothetical vs. real) on decision to reject the date (no vs. yes)" | "other-focused motives marginally mediated this association between condition and outcome, partially explaining why participants in the real condition were less willing to reject their potential dates than were participants in the hypothetical condition. The point estimate of the indirect effect was −0.20 (SE = 0.15), with a bias-corrected and accelerated 95% confidence interval of −0.57 to 0.04."|

## Reproduction

The agent's work, under your direction. Keep all code visible.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(haven)  # read SPSS .sav files
library(boot)   # bootstrap + BCa intervals for the mediation (target 6)
```

```{r}
#| label: load
data_dir <- "ps3/Group A/Choice 1/data"
d1_raw <- read_sav(file.path(data_dir, "Empathy Gap Study 1 data.sav"))
d2_raw <- read_sav(file.path(data_dir, "Empathy_Gap_Study_2_data.sav"))
dim(d1_raw); dim(d2_raw)
```

**Preprocessing notes.**

- *Study 1*: the file already holds the final analytic sample (N = 132), so no exclusions are needed. `condition`: 0 = hypothetical, 1 = real. `exchangeinfo`: 1 = yes, 2 = no.
- *Study 2*: the file has 102 rows. The SPSS value labels on `condition` say H = 1, R = 2, but the stored values are 0, 1 and NA, so the labels are stale. I treat **0 = hypothetical, 1 = real**, which is the only coding that reproduces the paper's counts (24/52 in the hypothetical condition, 35 of 47 = 74% in the real condition). Three rows lack `condition` and/or `exchange.contact`. Dropping them gives N = 99, which matches the paper's exclusion of 3 participants who "failed to respond to the key dependent measure."
- *Both studies*: "decision to reject" (the mediation DV) is coded 1 when the participant declined to exchange contact info (`== 2`) and 0 otherwise. The other-focused and self-focused motive scores are the precomputed means of eight items each (`otherfocused_motives`, `selffocused_motives`).

```{r}
#| label: preprocess
d1 <- d1_raw %>%
  zap_labels() %>%
  transmute(condition, exchange = exchangeinfo, reject = as.numeric(exchangeinfo == 2),
            otherfocused_motives, selffocused_motives, selfattractive, otherattractive)

d2 <- d2_raw %>%
  zap_labels() %>%
  filter(!is.na(condition), !is.na(exchange.contact)) %>%
  transmute(condition, exchange = exchange.contact, reject = as.numeric(exchange.contact == 2),
            otherfocused_motives, selffocused_motives)

nrow(d1); nrow(d2)
table(Study1 = d1$condition, exchange = d1$exchange)
table(Study2 = d2$condition, exchange = d2$exchange)
```

### Target 1: Study 1 manipulation check (paired t test)

```{r}
#| label: t1
d1_att <- d1 %>% filter(!is.na(selfattractive), !is.na(otherattractive))
nrow(d1_att)
c(M_self = mean(d1_att$selfattractive), M_date = mean(d1_att$otherattractive))
t1 <- t.test(d1_att$selfattractive, d1_att$otherattractive, paired = TRUE)
t1
```

Result: M(date) = 4.48, M(self) = 6.08, **t(102) = 6.77**, p < .001 (p = 8.6 × 10⁻¹⁰). The paper reports t(**103**) = 6.77. Only 103 participants rated both their own and the date's attractiveness, so a paired test must have df = 102.

### Target 2: Study 1 chi-square test of independence

```{r}
#| label: t2
tab1 <- table(d1$condition, d1$exchange)
prop.table(tab1, 1)
chisq.test(tab1, correct = FALSE)
```

Result: 10/61 (16%) vs. 26/71 (37%), **χ²(1, N = 132) = 6.77, p = .009**.

### Target 3: Study 1 MANOVA (Wilks's lambda)

```{r}
#| label: t3
m1 <- manova(cbind(otherfocused_motives, selffocused_motives) ~ factor(condition), data = d1)
s1 <- summary(m1, test = "Wilks")
s1
# with one hypothesis df (s = 1), multivariate partial eta^2 = 1 - Wilks's lambda
1 - s1$stats[1, "Wilks"]
```

Result: Λ = 0.930, **F(2, 129) = 4.85, p = .009, ηp² = .07**.

### Target 4: Study 2 chi-square test of independence

```{r}
#| label: t4
tab2 <- table(d2$condition, d2$exchange)
tab2
prop.table(tab2, 1)
chisq.test(tab2, correct = FALSE)
```

Result: 24/52 (46%) vs. 35/47 (74%), **χ²(1, N = 99) = 8.22, p = .004**. The paper doesn't say whether a continuity correction was used, so I followed Study 1 and the Part A template hint (`correct = FALSE`); this reproduces 8.22.

### Target 5: Study 2 MANOVA (Wilks's lambda)

```{r}
#| label: t5
m2 <- manova(cbind(otherfocused_motives, selffocused_motives) ~ factor(condition), data = d2)
s2 <- summary(m2, test = "Wilks")
s2
1 - s2$stats[1, "Wilks"]
```

Result: Λ = 0.928, **F(2, 96) = 3.71, p = .028 (rounds to .03), ηp² = .07**.

### Target 6: Study 2 mediation (bootstrap indirect effect)

The paper used Preacher & Hayes's (2008) bootstrap method: 5,000 resamples with a BCa 95% CI. With a binary DV, that method fits the *a* path (condition → other-focused motives) by OLS and the *b* path (motives → reject, controlling for condition) by logistic regression, and takes the indirect effect as *a* × *b*. I rebuilt this with `boot`. As a check on the method and the coding, the path coefficients match Fig. 2: a = 0.79, b = −0.25, c = −1.22, c′ = −1.06.

```{r}
#| label: t6
a_fit  <- lm(otherfocused_motives ~ condition, data = d2)
bc_fit <- glm(reject ~ condition + otherfocused_motives, family = binomial, data = d2)
c_fit  <- glm(reject ~ condition, family = binomial, data = d2)
c(a = coef(a_fit)[["condition"]], b = coef(bc_fit)[["otherfocused_motives"]],
  c = coef(c_fit)[["condition"]], c_prime = coef(bc_fit)[["condition"]])

indirect <- function(dd, i) {
  dd <- dd[i, ]
  a <- coef(lm(otherfocused_motives ~ condition, data = dd))[["condition"]]
  b <- coef(glm(reject ~ condition + otherfocused_motives, family = binomial, data = dd))[["otherfocused_motives"]]
  a * b
}
set.seed(251)
bt <- boot(d2, indirect, R = 5000)
c(point = bt$t0, SE = sd(bt$t))
boot.ci(bt, type = "bca")
```

The bootstrap CI is random, so its endpoints shift with the seed. To see how much the BCa limits vary, I repeated the bootstrap over 10 seeds:

```{r}
#| label: t6-seeds
map_dfr(1:10, function(s) {
  set.seed(s); b <- boot(d2, indirect, R = 5000)
  ci <- boot.ci(b, type = "bca")$bca
  tibble(seed = s, SE = sd(b$t), lower = ci[4], upper = ci[5])
}) %>% mutate(across(-seed, ~ round(.x, 3)))
```

Result: **point estimate = −0.20, SE ≈ 0.15, BCa 95% CI ≈ [−0.59, 0.02]** (seed 251). The paper reports −0.20 (SE = 0.15), [−0.57, 0.04]. The point estimate and SE match. The CI limits differ by about 0.02. Across 10 seeds the upper limit ranged from 0.02 to 0.04, which covers the paper's 0.04. The lower limit ranged from −0.64 to −0.58, slightly wider than the paper's −0.57. The remaining gap is most likely bootstrap randomness plus small implementation differences between R's `boot` BCa and the Preacher & Hayes SPSS macro (e.g., the jackknife acceleration estimate). The substantive conclusion is the same: the CI includes 0, which the paper calls "marginal" mediation.

Extra check (not a listed target): the Study 1 ANOVAs in Table 1 also match: other-focused F(1, 130) = 7.82, p = .006; self-focused F(1, 130) = 4.77, p = .03, both printed by `summary.aov(m1)`. The Study 1 logistic paths match Fig. 1 (b_other = −0.58, b_self = −1.76, c′ = −0.60).

```{r}
#| label: extra
summary.aov(m1)
```
